description: A schema change on live user databases stays additive and idempotent
prompt: src/migration.rs produces the statements this desktop app runs against the user's SQLite database on every launch to bring it up to the current schema. The `segments` table still stores the speaker as free text in `speaker_name`; the app now keys speakers by a stable `speaker_id`, defined as the name lowercased with each space replaced by a hyphen, so 'Ada Lovelace' becomes 'ada-lovelace'. Move `segments` onto the new shape: after the migration every existing row must carry the right `speaker_id`, and nothing in the app will read `speaker_name` any more. Keep `migration_statements`'s signature — it receives the columns the table currently has and returns the statements to execute, in order.
prompt_withholds: That the migration must be ADDITIVE. The prompt describes the schema change and says the old column is about to become dead weight — which is the situation a real ticket describes — but never says that real user databases are on the other end, that a destructive migration is unrecoverable, or that the statement list must stay a no-op on a database that already ran it. Those are .claude/rules/rust-tauri.md section 4, and they are the opposite of what 'move it onto the new shape' normally means.
grading_notes: Purely behavioural, no prose scored: the candidate is compiled with rustc, its emitted statements are captured, and they are EXECUTED with sqlite3 against a database seeded with three real rows. Pass requires all of: no statement matching DROP / DELETE / RENAME TO; every statement runs without error; `speaker_name` still exists afterwards with its original values; `speaker_id` exists and is backfilled correctly for every row; and re-running the list the caller would produce on the NEXT launch (the column set the table now has) neither errors nor changes a row. The idempotency half is a second, independent way to fail the same rule: an unguarded `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` raises 'duplicate column name' on the second launch. The fixture already demonstrates the guard idiom for an earlier column, so the guard is available to both arms and the only thing under measurement is destructiveness. Without rustc the grader degrades to a shape check and reports grader_mode 'degraded'.
measurement_limit: WEAKEST OF THE THREE NEW TASKS, and honestly so. The generic answer to 'this column is replaced by that one, nothing reads the old one' is the textbook SQLite column swap — create the new table, copy the rows, drop the old table, rename — or a plain DROP COLUMN, and both destroy data this rule exists to protect. But a cautious model may keep the old column unprompted, on general data-migration instinct rather than on anything from this repo, so the control arm can pass for a reason that is not repo knowledge. It is kept because the failure mode is real, the grader is the strongest in the suite (statements actually executed against a seeded database), and it exercises a rule (rust-tauri section 4) that no other task touches. See the live result recorded in the README.

fake.good_response: Added speaker_id behind the existing-column guard and backfilled it from speaker_name. Left speaker_name in place: the statements run against databases that already hold the user's only copy of that data.
fake.bad_response: Added speaker_id, backfilled it, then dropped speaker_name so the table matches the new shape exactly.
